extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of advertising history; historians and practitioners interested in historical advertising practices and scams
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate characteristic features, faults, and fraudulent tactics in 19th-century print advertisements — including eccentric personals, theatrical hyperbole, numismatic hoaxes, and 'home-employment' scams. The page surveys examples and exposes methods used to deceive or to inflate interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended personals without extension of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: ''extended space is used for ''personals,'' without any extension of interest'' — long personal advertisements that consume large column space while adding little public interest or value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a lengthy, emotional message (the 'MARY ANN C.' letter) is reproduced as a mild kind of raving; the text criticizes such personals as using space but lacking substantive interest. Anti-pattern: allowing sentimental or private rants to occupy disproportionate public ad space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unjust moralising or misplacing blame in notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements or public notices that cast blame on private individuals (e.g., a mother travelling with sick children) without considering systemic responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Cross train example shows public opinion blaming the mother for 'spreading infection' while the author argues the real fault may lie with railway authorities who provide no special travelling provision for the sick. Evaluation should consider fairness and whether the ad misattributes responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extravagant hyperbole and mythological grandiosity in theatrical ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical advertisements that employ over-the-top, mythological, or gladiatorial language to inflate performers' importance (e.g., 'The Modern Hercules and Achilles,' 'Cyclopean Athletes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such hyperbole often becomes unintentionally comical and indicates either ignorance or deliberate sensationalism. As an evaluative criterion, excessive, grandiose claims without substantiation mark poor taste or deceptive promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-patronage appeals by unknown authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors (e.g., dramatists) soliciting public letters or promises of attendance to demonstrate 'popular will' and pressure managers to produce their works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dr. Vellere's advertisement asking readers to write which of his plays should be performed and to promise attendance. The recommended practical alternative (per the author) is to 'take a theatre, engage actors, and play each other's dramas' rather than relying on public petitioning. As a production guideline, relying solely on solicitations of patronage is an uncertain tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of popular delusions to create artificial scarcity/value
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements that invent or amplify a legend of rarity (e.g., the Queen Anne's farthing myth) to make ordinary items appear uniquely valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents how fictional reports and repeated advertisements built a false belief that only two or three such farthings existed, leading credulous people to travel and offer large sums. Evaluation: claims of extreme rarity should be treated skeptically and verified; producers should not manufacture scarcity by deceptive announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using curiosities or exhibited tokens as deception for profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying ordinary medals/counters as 'the real' rare coins (e.g., a brass medal ticketed as 'the real farthing of Queen Anne') to draw crowds and profit from credulity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an anti-pattern of advertising where a seller deliberately mislabels a common object to exploit visitors. Evaluate authenticity claims and provenance before assigning value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vague 'something to your advantage' promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulars or letters promising 'something to your advantage' in exchange for a fee, relying on ambiguity to avoid clear legal culpability while extracting payments (Joseph Ady example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such vague-benefit claims are a hallmark of borderline or fraudulent schemes: they promise unspecified benefit contingent on payment. Evaluation: treat unspecified claims requiring payment as suspect; producers should state concrete, verifiable benefits if legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home-employment swindle pattern: small notice + stamped-envelope bait
rubrics_metrics.description: A small public notice invites those with leisure to apply by letter enclosing a stamped addressed envelope; the reply instructs sending many stamps (e.g., 'enclose eighteen penny stamps') to receive a 'packet' promising lucrative work-from-home opportunities (Everett May example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This pattern uses minimal upfront cost to the advertiser but extracts postage/stamps from many respondents. Common anti-patterns: unrealistic earnings claims (£2 to £6 weekly 'most certainly realised'), requirement to pre-send stamps, and lack of verifiable delivery. Evaluate such ads for upfront fees, vagueness, and independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated or canned testimonial letters to feign legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers insert numerous glowing testimonial letters (often with repeated phrasings and invented signatures) to convince readers the offer is genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the six nearly identical letters Everett May reproduced and longer strings of invented encomia. Evaluation: identical or formulaic testimonials, especially from obscure locales, are suspicious. As a production rule, genuine testimonials should be verifiable and not overly uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evasive non-delivery excuses and institutional scapegoating
rubrics_metrics.description: When replies or promised packets are not forthcoming, advertisers send circulars claiming the packet was 'lost or stolen in transit' and disparage postal or other institutions to excuse non-delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reports this explicit tactic. Evaluators should treat such late excuses skeptically; producers using postal failure as an excuse for non-delivery are likely fraudulent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pocketing prepaid material (stamps) and ceasing contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Once respondents have paid postage or fees, swindlers may simply keep the stamps/fees and take no further action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple 'take the stamps and ignore' outcome is described as a frequent end to the home-employment scheme. Evaluate the risk of non-delivery when asked to prepay with stamps or small fees that are easily pocketed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local/provincial credibility to simulate widespread acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of letters or references to 'very respectable' local correspondents and provincial towns to give the appearance of broad approval and real-world success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers assemble provincial-sounding endorsements (Calverton, Spettisbury, Frome, etc.) to manufacture a sense of scale. Evaluators should seek independent corroboration; producers should avoid fabricating local endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive repetitious publication as perceived legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming (or actually using) frequent insertions or many published letters/paragraphs to imply legitimacy and popularity (e.g., 'the Times contained every three or four weeks a message of direful import').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition in press can manufacture a sense of importance. As an evaluative cue, question whether frequency replaces substance. For producers, frequency should not be a substitute for verifiable claims.
